The Weight of Unsent Messages

I have a folder on my phone. It's called "Drafts" but it's really a graveyard. Forty-seven messages I started and abandoned. Some are apologies that felt too small for the wound. Some are declarations that felt too large for the room. One is just the word "hey" typed seventeen times, each instance deleted, each deletion a small death.

We don't talk about this, do we? The architecture of almost-communication. The way we build elaborate structures in our minds—conversations we rehearse in the shower, letters we compose at 3 AM, the perfect response we craft while the other person is still talking—and then we let them dissolve. Evaporate. Become nothing.

My grandmother kept a shoebox of unsent letters. I found it after she died, tied with a ribbon she'd saved from some anniversary, some gift. Inside were letters to her sister, who'd died in 1987. Letters to her husband, who'd died in 2003. Letters to me, written when I was twelve and angry about something I don't remember, something that felt like the end of the world. She never sent any of them. She told me once, when I was maybe twenty, that some things are better kept inside. "The saying makes it real," she said. "And real things have weight."

I didn't understand then. I thought she was being poetic, or sad, or both. Now I think she was describing a kind of mercy. The mercy of not making things permanent. Of letting them exist in the liminal space between thought and action, where they can't hurt anyone, where they can't be misunderstood, where they remain exactly what you intended rather than what the other person received.

But there's another mercy, isn't there? The mercy of sending. Of letting the weight exist in the world, of trusting that it can be held by someone else. I think about this when I read old text messages, the ones I actually sent. The clumsy ones. The ones sent at wrong moments, to wrong people, saying things I meant but didn't mean to mean in that way. They're embarrassing. They're human. They're proof that I was here, trying, failing, trying again.

The philosopher Emmanuel Levinas wrote about the face of the Other—the way another person's face calls you to responsibility, demands that you respond. I think about this when I'm tempted to delete. The face isn't there, not really. It's a screen, a cursor blinking. But the possibility of the face is there. The possibility that someone is waiting, that they need to hear this, that the weight of the unsent thing is crushing them too.

I sent one of those drafts last week. It was to someone I hurt, years ago, in a way I've never properly acknowledged. The draft had been sitting there for two years. I rewrote it eleven times. I almost deleted it again. But I sent it. And the response—not forgiveness, not yet, maybe never—was something else. It was acknowledgment. It was the beginning of a conversation that might, eventually, become a relationship again. Or might not. But it was real. It had weight. It existed outside my head.

My grandmother's letters are still in the shoebox. I keep it in my closet. Sometimes I read them. They're beautiful, in their way—full of love and regret and the particular loneliness of a woman who believed that some things should remain private. But I wonder, sometimes, what would have happened if she'd sent them. If her sister had known, before she died, that she was missed. If her husband had known, in his final years, that he was still loved. If I had known, at twelve, that she understood my anger, that she wasn't afraid of it, that she loved me through it.

The weight of unsent messages is a particular kind of grief. It's the grief of possible selves, possible relationships, possible versions of the world that never came to be. We carry it without naming it. We call it shyness, or pride, or wisdom. Sometimes it is those things. But sometimes it's just fear. The fear that the weight will be too much. The fear that we'll be misunderstood. The fear that the other person won't be able to hold what we're offering.

I'm trying to be braver. To send the messages. To let them have weight. To trust that the world can hold more than I think it can. It's not easy. The drafts folder is still full. But it's smaller now. Forty-three messages instead of forty-seven. Progress, of a sort. The kind that doesn't show up in any metric, that no one else can see. The kind that matters anyway.

There's a poem by Mary Oliver that I return to, about a man who finds a snake in his path and, instead of killing it, lets it pass. "I had no right, I knew, to leave it there," he says. "To let it escape into the world." I think about this when I delete. When I let something escape into the world of almost, of not-quite, of never-was. The snake is still there, in the grass. It's still real. But it's not in the world I have to be responsible for.

I want to be responsible. I want to let things escape into the world and stay there. To be changed by them. To change others. This is the work, I think. Not the perfection of the message, but the sending. Not the guarantee of understanding, but the risk of it. Not the weightlessness of the draft, but the gravity of the sent.

My grandmother is gone now. Her letters remain. I read them and I feel her presence, her particular way of loving—careful, contained, real in its own bounded way. But I also feel the absence of what might have been. The conversations that never happened. The weight that never got shared.

I don't want to end up like that. I don't want my closet to be full of shoeboxes. I want to send. I want to be misunderstood. I want to hold other people's weight, and let them hold mine. It's terrifying. It's necessary. It's the only way I know to be fully here, in this world, with these people, in this time that we have and won't have again.

The cursor blinks. The draft waits. I will write something. I will send it. I will let it be real.
